title: Ryan Hance
notes:
So my plan for this content is to first run through a very high level view of my background, then dive deeper into two areas of work that I believe to be relevant to this role.
We will primarily spend time on my work at Bayer because it is most in line with what I understand to be the shape of this role, and then we will wrap up with some of my work at Delta Airlines because it speaks a little deeper to my leadership in the design strategy context.
After that, some time to dive deeper on anything I mentioned or didn’t mention.
I’ll leave you with some fun links at the end to explore some of what I spoke about as well, in case you still have any curiosity left over.

title: Career Part 1
notes:
My career actually started in film and television on the producing and operations side.
Essentially, I worked with clients to get clear on their vision then determine what was realistic with the budget and timeline they were able to offer.
Then I would work with the production teams to figure out how to make that vision a reality in the timeline and budget that was offered.
Then I would lead those teams on set, making that vision a reality and problem solving hundreds of issues live every day.
I developed a great mind for using frameworks for rapid decision making, communicating well, and most importantly, I had to see the entire system and how it affected every possible stakeholder in every choice that was made.
Throughout this time, I also helped a lot of teams onboard to the modern technology era, helping teams adopt tools for collaborating and visualizing the systems of a crew, a scene, or a story.
I had gotten into this industry because I was a creative, but I was thriving in the industry because I was quick to understand the business side of the work.
I realized that there was something really fun about the intersection of creativity and business and that real business and operations work was all a creative effort anyway.
I recognized that ultimately the industry wasn’t where I wanted to be long term and I decided to go back to school to try to understand a little bit more of what I was uncovering with my passion for the intersection of business, creativity, and systems thinking.

title: Career Part 2
notes:
I found the perfect degree.
It’s called Creative Business Leadership, but it was really service design and design strategy crossed with an MBA, including financial modeling, marketing, and all of the typical MBA classes, but also design research, business modeling, product and service strategy, etc.
During this program, I started my design strategy career professionally with a start up that did logistics for universities,
helping them develop a new education-as-a-service offering for their university partners,
building both the business model and the design of the program together so that one informed the other at every turn.
This was the first time I got to really see that design is one of the greatest business solutions 
and a viable career path for someone with more of a business background.
I was then brought in as a design strategist at a small studio that was partnering with Delta Airlines for a global sustainability project, which we will chat about that towards the end of this.
After that project, I got my biggest and most dynamic challenge so far. I was hired as a design strategist and design thinking facilitator at Bayer in the Crop Sciences division of the Fortune 500 global employer.
Bayer is where we will spend the bulk of our time today, but before we get into that, I will quickly wrap up my career path with my most recent experience which was
leading strategy at a construction science start up using a design thinking foundation and design frameworks and tools to develop the business model, the hiring funnel, and playbooks and processes that the company ran on.
and most recently, I’ve spent the last three years partnering with franchisee and franchisor clients be the strategic voice behind organizational change, technology implementations, and business cases for new offerings.
I know that seems like a long and varied path, but I share it because I think it really all points the same direction. 
I find gaps in end-to-end experiences, map the system so everyone can see it, speak about it, and make aligned decisions, then I build roadmaps that get business, design, and technical folks to the same destination together. 
One that serves both the end user and the business.

title: Bayer Crop Sciences
notes:
So, there are two job contexts I wanted to tell you about today that I think speak to my strengths in a role like this, one that requires a strategist to be dynamic, see the business case and the perspective, and be able to articulate ideas and influence across different stakeholder groups.
Both of the things I am going to speak to were at the Fortune 500 level, but I have a lot of experience with startups and middle market businesses as well, which I am happy to touch on at the end.
What I am going to talk about first is some of my work at Bayer, then I will speak to some work at Delta Airlines.
So context for this case study is that I was in Bayer’s Crop Sciences division, responsible for only a third of their business, but still tens of billions in revenue.
Bayer Crop Science, which I will just be referring to as Bayer going forward sells to farmers as their ultimate end use, but some of the other personas I worked with there included scientists, researchers, operators, sales, customer service, agronomists, and brand specific market teams.
I was originally hired as a Design Strategist and Design Thinking Facilitator, where my focus was going to be to represent the voice of the farmer in the end-to-end grower digital experience.
I sat right at the intersection of business, technologists, and design.
The primary job was turning user understanding into user stories, and helping business and technologists prioritize what to build based on user empathy and being clear on what the end user actually needs, when, and from who.

title: The End-to-End Farmer Experience
notes:
Great, so the end-to-end grower digital experience…
This was all public facing sites, the pre-auth portal pages, and the grower portal on the other side of login where most of the farmer’s work was done.
This is global by the way. We were building it for North America, but working in tandem with the EMEA, APAC, and LATAM teams to help them determine essentially what face they were going to put on top of it in their relevant countries. And I was the one who would be consulted in those contexts. Me and our UI designer.
These digital properties were the access points for every other persona in the company that I just referenced — sales, agronomy, distribution, etc.
It was a full omni-channel digital experience where everyone had a strong, global, revenue-focused agenda, and I had to be the voice of the only persona that wasn’t actually in the build conversations.
So my challenge was to ensure that the product that was getting built was actually being built for the end user, and not for cash grabs, otherwise retention would fail and there would be no users left to sell to.

title: My Position
notes:
The bigger business challenge in this context though, was that the farmer-facing product was being designed by outside consultancies, from what business stakeholders told them. There was no direct study of the actual farmers that would be using the product.
My job was to discover what secondary-stakeholder-sourced strategy could not find, like what the end users actually believed, desired, and needed, and influence how things get designed and built towards those truths.
So as you can imagine with this level of complexity, a lot of insights were derived, and a lot more business challenges were discovered.
I want to quickly showcase a few different ways in which I approach problems and the types of solutioning I come up with, and if at the end we have time and interest, I can dive in a bit deeper.
All of this will be connected to this end-to-end experience work and prioritizing users.
The following problem contexts are ordered from most end-user-focused at the forefront to more global, standards focused at the end.

title: Recognizing Misaligned Paradigms
notes:
So when I arrived, our technologists were actively building the MVP of the end to end farmer experience, based off of the design requirements developed by the external consultancy who were making recommendations based off of standard templates their company used and the input derived from what they were calling user testing.
When I arrived, and studied our internal documentation about the farmers, including their growing journeys, customer feedback, and anything else I could get my hands, I recognized quickly that the screens and recommendations from the consultancy felt very off from my understanding of the end users.
When I started pushing back on some recommendations, and showing them the internal proof points that my push back was coming from, I uncovered that all of their input and what they were calling user research was all from three ex-farmers.
Two problems with that:
Three is not a statistically relevant number, and every decision was being made from it. And
Ex-farmers are not the end users of this product. Most of these guys they were talking to probably weren't even using technology at this scale when they were still farming.
I could speak to a lot of what that meant for how we had to restructure ways of working and develop gates for validating research, and rewrite every user story that had been shipped to the engineering and build teams,
But what I would like to focus on is one specific business challenge that I think is important to speak about in this age of AI and building products and services that have AI integrated in some form or fashion.

title: Trust
notes:
For clarity, this product did not have AI at the time, but when we are talking about building for AI, the primary thing I think about is building for end user trust.
And this project was a space where trust was about to be obliterated if we shipped as is.
See, the consultancy was primarily a marketing consultancy, and in a lot of ways, the end-to-end farmer experience was a marketing product.
It was a space to provide farmers with tools that they needed, but also access for Bayer’s internal teams to reach those users.
As a designer with a business mindset, I want to provide a product or service that creates a recurring usage model and promotes the returning of a customer to our business.
To do that well, you have to build trust at a level that creates retention.
What I recognized was happening, is that the business stakeholders and the consultancy were primarily focused on getting data from the customers to sell better products to them.
Now there is nothing wrong with that. I personally always click Allow when Apple asks if it can share my data with the app I just downloaded, because
I want the best experience and I want you tell about products and services I might like, because I bet they will make my life better!
And you probably already have access to my data anyway. It’s 2026. 
But I am not a farmer who is technology averse and politically untrusting of large corporations.
Those were the big insights I discovered when studying our end users, and with that lens, it’s a little bit easier to see, that these personas require a little bit more time, patience, and human touchpoints to develop trust with a company like this.
I started realizing that this team was making a lot of big data asks like farm size, location, revenue, employees, etc etc — all of these things that feel a bit personal to the farmer.
And worse, these asks were landing up front, as a requirement to get into the portal and use the product.
Again, valuable information for the business to have.
Requested at the wrong point in the journey.
They were hemorrhaging users before the users even made it in the door.

title: Designing for Trust
notes:
So after uncovering some farmer personas that had been created before my arrival, and some customer feedback that spoke to this issue of data sharing comfortability, I shared this with the business stakeholders.
And framed the business problem for them — Users weren’t going to make it to the door with much trust, much less through it.
And if we can’t get them to the door or through the door, then we don’t have customers to retain. And our business model is dependent on retaining customers through all phases of the growing cycle and over multiple seasons.
Then I made my recommendations:
Keep every data ask. Even ask for more.
We just have rearrange where and when this data is being requested.
It is even more of a win if we can tie a business win for them to us having this data.
As in, showing a farmer what we can calculate automatically for their seed requirements and crop yields based on understanding the size of their farm.
Or connecting our seed recommendations specific to the hyper-regional, niche soil that they are working with based on the location they provide.
So there’s a time, a place, and a purpose behind every data ask. When you do that, trust becomes inherent, because they visualize themselves winning and understand how we come into that ability to win.
So I worked with the team to plot the data ask points across the farmer’s journey, and then mapped those journey points to the relevant screens and areas of the grower portal that they would be interacting with.
In good design, everybody wins.

title: Other Relevant Roles
notes:
A few notes on this:
I led the UX writing recommendations in these data ask point to help articulate the win for the farmer that they would see in their UI.
I additionally surfaced about 35% more product and service opportunities within the end to end experience than were developed by the consultancy in my first two months.
I love writing, so I also — as a design strategist really should — wrote all of the user stories throughout build, testing, launch, and feedback, for our teams to be able to understand the needs of the farmer from their perspective.
I wrote acceptance criteria for User Acceptance Testing and led that UAT with my research partner for the North American user base.

title: CDP Work
notes:
So I had been looking at this from the UI layer. Now it was time to really dive deep into the data layer and understand what we could really do with data that have or don’t have.
In parallel to this work, the marketing team requested a Customer Data Platform. From what I could understand, every other Fortune 100 had one, and we *just had to have it.*
The business challenge was that there was a decision that was made very high up to buy a Customer Data Platform at the enterprise level, but no one was sure which one to buy or what to do with it.
So it became my job to figure those things out.
I spoke about this project in depth in my last conversation with the team, so my intention is not go in depth again on this, but to show another angle of leading strategy in this end to end experience that is truly focused on end users while also understanding business priorities and strategies for increasing revenue.
I was essentially asked to figure out how we could use this to collect and strategically use more data from our users, and which tool would help us do that the best.
I realized that this was another opportunity to design with users at the forefront in a way that also helped the business.
It was the same trust work that was previously coming from work with business stakeholders, now with technology stakeholders.
When I recognized that, I mapped every touchpoint where a CDP could reach a farmer onto our 6 phase journey map from planning to harvest.
Then I wrote every use case from the farmer’s perspective. Using the farmer’s desires at each decision point correlated with what sharing data with Bayer could help them do and how it would make them successful.
I wrote requirements for building trust with a tool like this, what we could collect, why each thing we collected could help the users, and how to articulate those wins for the farmer to help them make the decision to more freely offer up their data.
I then created a Tool Criteria Canvas complete with open questions for vendors to help them decide which company’s CDP to go with. Though I did recommend Adobe’s based on what I thought it could do from my research and that it was easily integrated into our tech stack.
I also realized there was a level of governance required that wasn’t being considered. The current plan was to have a single person responsible for all aspects of this tool. I believed a CDP required a team to really create the business and user value that this tool had the potential for.
So I developed a 12 person team structure and governance model for creating value long term and shared that out with my recommendations as well.
Ultimately, Bayer did select Adobe and build a team around the tool.

title: Global, Enterprise-Level Service Blueprinting
notes:
A big part of this CDP work was actually understanding our tech stack for the first time, and mapping how we collect data throughout our tech stack.
This work uncovered some real redundancies and gaps.
See, Bayer Crop Science had grown about ten times their size in about 10 years through acquisitions — most famously, they acquired Monsanto after they had gone bankrupt after growing ten times their size via acquisitions.
There had been some laying off of teams from acquired companies here and there, but no real reconciling of all of the teams and tech stacks that now did similar work across the organization.
The business problem I recognized as I was doing this uncovering of our tech stack for the CDP opportunities was that Bayer had bought duplicate tools doing similar things just in different regions, parallel teams solving the same problems for slightly different personas, and tons of gaps where one team assumed another team was taking care of it.
There was no ability to look at the entire business and how all of our tools, processes, and people integrated.
This was the beginning of what became known as the Global, Enterprise-Level Service Blueprinting Effort.
I was brought on to help with this and we determined that the only way to map all of this appropriately was to build it on top of the general 6 phase journey of the farmer.
If everything pointed at how it served the end user, we were going to be able to easily see redundancies, gaps, and opportunities.
Me being the design representative of the farmer, I became a leader of this project without any real authority, because ultimately I was the only helping the other strategists and researchers figure out how their tools, processes, and people connected back to the farmer’s journey.
Ultimately, a team of 8 of us dug into the deepest depths of the company across 5 primary countries that represented their region, and built this enterprise-wide service blueprint with over 20,000 data points.
That was uncovering the redundancies, gaps, and opportunities of the present state.
I then led the duplication and redevelopment of the blueprint as a future state roadmap with recommendations of what teams, technologies, and processes to consolidate and what opportunities are available based on the gaps and how to prioritize them.
About a month ago I heard from my old boss that leadership is still using it to make decisions.

title: Design Standards
notes:
As I mentioned, the service blueprinting effort opened up our radar as a design team to a lot of teams, personas, and tools that we had not previously been aware of or designing for.
We discovered that a lot of these teams were using old design standards, external consultants, and even engineers to make design decisions on the products they were shipping.
We quickly realized that our little design team was not big enough to be everywhere we needed to be and that there was a ton of inconsistency across brands, regions, and products.
The end to end farmer experience was now the design standard as it was the most recent and only omni-channel experience in our repertoire, but that standard only reached the tools that got integrated into that experience already
And this was all on the Customer Platform, not touching our Operations Platform, our Research Platform, the Design Studio, or the COE.
This inconsistency in an enterprise where our products and services greatly vary in terms of design and technical maturity was going to be a big business challenge for showing up with consistency in front of our end users.
I brought this realization to the Head of Design for Customer Platforms and he tasked me with gathering all of the designers and leading workshops to develop design principles, subprinciples, and ways of working that ensure these standards.
I started with the Heads of Design for all five business units, designing a workshop to help them determine who Bayer Crop Science’s wanted to be from a design perspective moving forward.
Then I brought in our most relevant design leaders, those who had direct reports under them to uncover the subprinciples that would guide us in understanding how those principles impact the day to day of our work.
After that, I worked with the mass of individual contributors to develop the processes and ways of working that would allow us to deliver these principles consistently.
Using this three step method allowed for buy in at all levels and for the principles through processes to be developed by the relevant stakeholders enforcing them.
After a few weeks of workshops and the processes shown in these pictures, we landed on clear and well articulated Design Standards that were relevant across all three platforms, the design studio, and the COE, and mapped the ownership of these standards to the relevant stakeholders across all teams.
We gained adoption across all of these business units, and across all of our regions, meaning that teams and countries I had never met could now make design decisions that aligned across languages and continents.

title: Agentic Personas
notes:
Another business challenge that came up during our global blueprinting effort was the discovery that most teams were making choices when designing or building products and services without having any access at all to the users or having a design strategist embedded within their team.
Across the organization, users were being gatekept from designers by the business stakeholders and a lot technical teams were left with no access at all.
There were only 5 or 6 design strategists and there were hundreds of teams. So teams tended to not have a design thinking person either which lowered the general level of user empathy.
Us design strategists certainly couldn’t be everywhere, and if teams had no access to users, then they were making decisions that would affect their end users indefinitely… entirely based on assumption.
Luckily, I had a good understanding of what data we had access to internally. We had been collecting so much data from any team we could about their users for the blueprint.
And it was January 2023. I had just spent an entire month playing with ChatGPT as much as possible, really discovering what might be possible and how it might integrate into my daily workflow.
I was very early on Chat and very enthusiastic about it, even though all of the language that was being used in the company was that we needed to be very careful with AI and all of the people in the design org had a lot of fear and animosity towards it.
Luckily, my boss was very innovative, and when I told her I thought I could use AI to help teams make decisions by essentially creating fake users, she could see the benefit that that might bring to teams who were extremely disconnected from the end user.
She asked me if I could prove it without using any of Bayer’s data and that is when I built my first agentic persona via the OpenAI API.
At the time, agents were not a thing. We had no clue what this could be, so we were calling them proto-personas. Simply a prototype of a real persona.
She did some internal research and found a team that was working on building an internal LLM platform for the company to use that wouldn’t openly share our data.
I got connected in with them, showed them the MVP, and ultimately got to build these out at scale internally.
I had a vision that teams would be able to chat with these agents via Microsoft Teams, where they already spent their time, but Copilot didn’t even exist yet.
I worked with that team to create a knowledge base for the proto-personas, made some persona characters, and wired it up into Teams chats so that people could use it.
Before any improvements to this crazy idea, I had subject matter experts with over 20 years of experience at the company rating their persona at over 80% accurate.
UAT failures dropped and the entire organization’s design maturity rose because people were finally connected to their end users for the first time in their career with Bayer.
And then a lot of my work became design strategy for AI from there.

title: Dynamic Work
notes:
Now, we just covered a lot of topics.
End-user-centric design, designing for trust, customer data platforms, global enterprise level service blueprinting, design standards, and agentic persons.
I brought all of this to the table, because I believe a design strategist’s role is meant to be extremely dynamic.
That every day, it could be going a different direction, solving a different problem that ultimately affects a business’ revenue, and they need to be able to speak to and focus on that, always understanding how the decisions they make sit at the intersection of the user and the business.
We have to be dynamic, understanding the user primarily, but also the business, and the tech stack all at the same time.
The difference between a disposable camera and an IMAX camera is dynamic range: how many shades it can hold between pure white and pure black.
Any camera can capture the subject.
But an IMAX camera pulls detail out of the places that look blown out or pitch black.
Any design strategist can map a journey.
A dynamic strategist finds the business opportunities, better ways of working, and money left on the table that’s hiding in the shadows.
All of the Bayer work I just spoke to came off of one core project, the end-to-end farmer experience.
From a consultancy lens, my intention of structuring this information in this way is to point to the fact that there is always another problem to be solved where design strategy can be the solution.
I believe that a big sell of who I am is that I can find that high priority issue that no one is paying attention to, frame the need and the win to the right people, and create opportunities for more work.

title: Business Design Strategist
notes:
Now, this is a little less user-centric by the typical definition, but in my eyes, stakeholders are users too, and a good design strategist needs to be able to align work with their needs as well.
So, Delta had about 3,000 to 5,000 retired beverage carts sitting in a warehouse somewhere in South Atlanta
They were also very much trying to market that they were a sustainable brand.
At the time, they had a very short lived program where they were voluntarily paying non-profits to offset their carbon footprint.
Now, its more of a “Yeah, we are super sustainable, you can pay us more for your flight to offset our carbon emissions.”
In the midst of this pre-COVID pro-sustainability effort, they hired a creative studio to find these dead beverage carts a second life.
I was the dedicated business design strategist on a team of sixteen creatives from 8 countries and 9 disciplines.
Delta gave us no direction on purpose. They were excited to see how creative we could get. All they said they wanted was to find a second life for their beverage carts.
A very fun business challenge for a group of creatives.

title: Design Strategy Frameworks for Alignment
notes:
Our second big meeting with them was to present concepts that the team had developed.
The ideas were wildly creative, very impressive if possible, but I didn’t see much business value in most of them.
It was hard for me to express that at the time.
I was new to the team and had trouble at the time helping these extremely enthusiastic creatives see their ideas from Delta’s perspective.
When we had this presentation with the Delta team, they did not see the business value in these creative ideas.
I sat and listened.
I listened to how they spoke about the project and what the gaps were between our ideas and theirs.
I recognized that my team didn’t have a good grasp on who the stakeholders were that we were actually designing for.
I drew a 2x2 on the whiteboard and asked Delta: are these the people we are designing for?
When they said yes, their team finally felt seen, and my team realized I might know what I was talking about, and I realized that visualizing information with frameworks is one of the best ways to communicate.
I realized that the real end user was Delta's executive team and the real job was sustainability marketing.
We needed to be marketable at scale, which meant it needed to cost the business less to launch and sustain whatever idea we came up with, than the value it brought in.

title: Strategic Shifts
notes:
When we got back to the studio, I printed a business model canvas really big and put it on the wall.
From then on, we walked every concept we had through it block by block: channels, end users, jobs to be done, feasibility at 3 to 5 thousand units.
I led the structuring of the team's goals into nine design criteria, later boiling them down to three.
Twenty concepts became ten. Ten concepts became five. And at the end, our remaining concepts each had a real business case and big marketing win.
The recommendation I pitched was turning the carts into hydroponic gardens for teaching sustainability in Georgia classrooms.
Partner with Home Depot — another Atlanta based Fortune 50 and create a kit that fits inside the cart that the companies can donate to classrooms.
You sell the donation opportunity to other companies under the pretense that they can invest in their local community, then Delta and Home Depot have the costs covered.
But the big win is that once they donate it, it’s a tax write off anyway and they make a ton of money on the back of the connected marketing campaign.
It’s simple business, a win-win-win, an easy yes.

title: Why EPAM Continuum
notes:
Right now, I am in a position where I am sourcing work, developing strategy for said work, and then implementing.
After three years of doing this, two things have become abundantly clear:
Strategy is absolutely where I have the most fun.
I miss being part of a team.
I want to return to influencing laterally and longitudinally. 
Right now most of my influencing is primarily with CEOs, C suites, and GMs which is awesome, don’t get me wrong. 
A lot to learn from that, but there are more levels to impact when you are working at scale and not the sole implementation piece. 
I am like a little kid when it comes to this type of work. Strategy is where I play. Design tools are my toys. And like a child, there is no singular sandbox that can contain me. I can have fun anywhere.
I need an environment that is conducive to that.
A consultancy, especially one as storied as Continuum — a team I would be really excited to learn from, is the perfect environment where different problems come across your desk regularly.
